title: The End Has Come for the Land
overview: In short, urgent bursts of poetry, Ezekiel announces that judgment is about to fall on the whole land of Israel, and that nothing the people trust in will save them.

parts.label: The end has come (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Ezekiel, living among the exiles in Babylon, announces that the end of the nation as it stood is arriving everywhere at once; "the four corners" means every part of the land. God says he will hold back pity and let the people's own conduct come back on them.

parts.label: A disaster like no other (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: The words pile up and repeat, like an alarm shouted again and again. The mention of the mountains may picture harvest songs or festival celebrations on the hills turning to panic, though scholars are unsure of the exact image.

parts.label: The rod has budded (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: The rod that sprouts and grows is most likely the Babylonian army, slowly ripening into the tool of punishment, though some read the pride blossoming beside it as Israel's own. Land sold in hard times normally returned to the family every fiftieth year, but here buying and selling lose all meaning because invaders will take everything.

parts.label: No one will fight (vv. 14-18)
parts.note: The trumpet calls soldiers to battle, but terror leaves everyone too weak to go, while war waits outside the walls and hunger and disease kill inside. Survivors hide in the hills moaning like doves, and put on rough sackcloth and shave their heads, common signs of grief.

parts.label: Silver and gold are useless (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: People will throw their money into the streets because it cannot buy food or safety, and the very jewelry they were proud of had been used to make idols. The place God treasures most is usually taken to be the temple in Jerusalem, which foreign plunderers will break into and defile.

parts.label: Chains and failing leaders (vv. 23-27)
parts.note: The call for a chain points to captives being led away together, a grim end for a land described as full of bloodshed and violence. Prophets, priests, elders and king all fail, and God says he will judge the people according to their conduct and what they deserve.

disagreement: Christians agree this describes Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, but differ on whether "the end" also looks ahead to later events or a final judgment of the world, or should be read only within its own historical moment.
think: Is there a real difference between being punished and simply facing the results of what you have done, and how would you tell the two apart?
